sections.title: Prologue
sections.html:
Prologue

The water is black at night. That's the thing nobody tells you about lakes up north. In daylight they're postcards, blue and silver and ringed with pine. But after dark the surface turns to oil, and anything that goes under simply stops existing.

I know this better than most people.

I was seventeen the first time I watched someone disappear beneath dark water. I'm thirty-one now, and I have spent fourteen years not thinking about it. Not thinking about the way the ripples closed like a mouth. Not thinking about how long I stood on the edge before I moved.

So when a woman I'd never met offered me six thousand dollars to spend six weeks alone in a house on a lake, I should have said no.

But I was broke. And I was desperate. And she had a list of rules that made it all sound so simple.

Nine rules.

I broke every one of them.

sections.title: Chapter 1
sections.html:
Chapter 1

Rule #1: Feed Juniper at seven and seven. Never skip.

The video call connects on the third try, because the Wi-Fi in Tasha's apartment is held together with prayer and a router older than her cat.

"Nora Vance?"

The woman on my laptop screen is beautiful in the way that costs money. Pale hair pulled into a low knot, a cream sweater, skin that has never known a fluorescent office light. Behind her, through a wall of windows, I can see water and trees.

"That's me," I say. I've angled the laptop so she can't see the sleeping bag balled on the end of Tasha's couch, or the stack of envelopes on the coffee table stamped FINAL NOTICE in red.

"Celeste Aldridge." She smiles. "Thank you for making time."

As if I have anything but time. Four months ago I was a paralegal at a firm in downtown Minneapolis. Then I misfiled a single document in a custody case, a partner lost a motion he should have won, and suddenly my desk was in a cardboard box and my name was poison in every law office in the Twin Cities.

"Your references were glowing," Celeste says. "Mrs. Patterson in Edina said you were the best house sitter she's ever had."

Mrs. Patterson in Edina is Tasha, who is currently hiding in her bedroom eleven feet away, and who put on a very convincing old-lady voice when Celeste called her yesterday.

"That's kind of her," I say.

"My husband and I are leaving for Portugal on Friday. Six weeks. We have a dog, Juniper, and a house that doesn't like to be empty." She tilts her head. "It's remote. Lake Tamarack, about four hours north of you. The nearest town is Pell, and Pell is mostly a gas station and a bar. Does that bother you?"

"Not at all. I like quiet."

"Good." Something moves in her eyes, some private calculation. "Because it's very quiet. Some people find that difficult."

"I won't."

"The pay is six thousand dollars. Half up front."

I keep my face very still. Six thousand dollars is two months of rent, the minimum payment on my credit cards, and the orthodontist bill I still owe from when I was a kid and my mother put it in my name. Six thousand dollars is breathing room.

"That's very generous," I say.

"I'm paying for reliability." Celeste leans closer to her camera. "There are rules, Nora. They're not complicated, but they're not optional. I'll email them to you tonight. If you can't follow them, tell me now and we'll part as friends."

"I can follow rules."

This is not true. My entire life has been a series of rules I bent until they broke. But I say it with such confidence that I almost believe it.

Celeste watches me for a long moment. Then she smiles again, wider this time.

"Yes," she says. "I think you're exactly who I'm looking for."

* * *

The email arrives at 11:52 p.m. No greeting. No signature. Just a list.

1. Feed Juniper at seven and seven. Never skip.

2. Never let anyone inside. No matter who they say they are.

3. The landline will ring at nine every night. Answer it. Say "All quiet." Hang up.

4. The third floor is closed. Don't go up.

5. The lights facing the lake stay on from dusk to dawn.

6. No photos of the house. Not online. Not anywhere.

7. If Grant calls your cell, do not answer.

8. Burn nothing in the fireplace.

9. Never go to the boathouse.

I read it three times. Tasha reads it over my shoulder, her breath smelling like boxed wine.

"Okay, number seven is insane," she says. "Grant is her husband, right? Why wouldn't you answer the husband?"

"Maybe they're getting divorced."

"And they're going to Portugal together?" She taps number nine. "And what's in the boathouse? A body?"

"It's probably rotten boards. Insurance thing."

"Nora." Tasha sits on the arm of the couch. "This is weird. This is true-crime-podcast weird."

"This is six thousand dollars weird," I say, and I close the laptop.

That night I dream about water. I always do when I'm anxious. In the dream I am standing on a rock ledge above a quarry, and my little sister is waving at me from the middle of the black pool, and she's laughing, and then she isn't.

I wake at four in the morning with my heart slamming and the taste of pennies in my mouth.

Three days later, I drive north.

sections.title: Chapter 2
sections.html:
Chapter 2

Rule #3: The landline will ring at nine every night. Answer it. Say "All quiet." Hang up.

The house is not a house. It's a statement.

It rises from the pines at the end of a mile-long gravel drive, three stories of glass and dark cedar, cantilevered over the slope so that the whole thing seems to lean toward the water, like it's listening. Lake Tamarack spreads out below it, gray and restless under an October sky.

At the bottom of the slope, where a long wooden dock runs into the lake, sits a small building with a steep roof and a green door. The boathouse. Even from here I can see the padlock.

Celeste meets me in the driveway. In person she's taller than I expected, and colder, like the temperature drops a degree when she steps close.

"You found it," she says. "Most people miss the turn."

"Your directions were good."

"They're always good." She hands me a ring of keys, each one tagged with a colored dot. "Front, back, garage, shed. The house alarm code is on the fridge. Juniper is inside. She's shy with strangers, but she'll warm to you."

"Is your husband here? I'd love to meet him."

The smallest pause. "Grant went ahead to Minneapolis. We fly out of MSP tonight." She glances at her watch, slim and gold. "Which means I have to go. Everything you need is on the kitchen counter."

"Wait, is there anything else I should know about the rules? Number four, the third floor—"

"It's closed." She's already opening the door of a white Range Rover. "Nora. The rules are the job. Follow them, and in six weeks you'll have six thousand dollars and a lovely story about the peaceful autumn you spent on a lake."

She says peaceful the way other people say good luck.

Then she's gone, tires crunching down the gravel, and I'm alone with a house that watches me with a hundred glass eyes.

* * *

Juniper is a gray-muzzled golden retriever mix who takes one look at me and hides under the dining table.

"Hi, sweetheart," I say, crouching. "I'm Nora. I'm the new one."

She thumps her tail once, which I decide to take as a welcome.

The inside of the house is even more intimidating than the outside. Polished concrete floors. A kitchen the size of Tasha's whole apartment, with an island of white marble and a range with eight burners. A living room two stories tall, where a stone fireplace rises to the ceiling beside a wall of windows looking out on the lake. Everything is clean and expensive and weirdly empty, like a furniture showroom. No family photos. No mail on the counter. No shoes by the door.

On the counter there's a binder labeled HOUSE, a bag of dog food, and a single sheet of paper with the nine rules printed on it. Someone has already stuck a copy to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a loon.

I explore. The second floor has four bedrooms, each more beautiful and anonymous than the last. Mine, according to a sticky note on the door, is the one at the end of the hall, with a view of the dock.

At the end of the second-floor landing, a staircase continues upward. At the top of it there's a door. Solid wood, dark stain, a brass deadbolt.

I stand at the bottom of those stairs for a long time.

The third floor is closed. Don't go up.

"Fine," I say out loud, and my voice echoes back to me off the glass. "I wasn't going to."

* * *

At seven, I feed Juniper, who eats like she's been starving for a year. At seven-thirty, the sun sinks behind the trees across the lake, and I go through the house turning on every light that faces the water, the way rule five says. The house becomes a lantern. I imagine how it must look from across the bay. Anybody out there would be able to see everything.

I try not to think about that.

At 8:59 p.m., I'm sitting at the kitchen island with a glass of Celeste's wine, staring at the cordless landline on its cradle by the pantry.

At 9:00 exactly, it rings.

I let it ring twice, just to prove to myself I can. Then I pick it up.

"Hello?"

Silence on the other end. Not dead air. Someone breathing.

"Hello? This is Nora—"

"Say it."

Celeste's voice. Low and even.

My mouth is suddenly dry. "All quiet."

The line clicks off.

I stand in the kitchen with the phone in my hand, listening to the house hum around me. Juniper whines from under the table.

"It's fine," I tell her. "She's just checking in. That's a normal thing people do."

Above me, on the third floor, something creaks.

It's an old sound, a house-settling sound, the sound of cedar contracting in the cold. That's all.

I go to bed with the door locked anyway.

sections.title: Chapter 3
sections.html:
Chapter 3

Rule #6: No photos of the house. Not online. Not anywhere.

In the morning the lake is covered in mist, and I almost feel stupid about last night.

In daylight, the house is just a house. An absurdly nice house, but a house. I make coffee in a machine that costs more than my car. I take Juniper out on the lawn and throw a tennis ball she refuses to fetch. I walk down the slope toward the water, and stop fifty feet from the boathouse, and turn around.

Not because I'm scared. Because rule nine.

After breakfast I drive into Pell for groceries. Celeste was right: it's a gas station, a bar called the Tamarack Tap, a Lutheran church, a post office, and a small grocery store called Halvorsen's with a hand-painted sign. The whole town smells like woodsmoke and lake water.

Inside Halvorsen's, a teenage cashier with a nose ring looks up from her phone. "You're not from here."

"That obvious?"

"Everybody's from here." She scans my bread. "Summer people are gone by Labor Day. So you're either lost or you're a hunter, and you don't look like a hunter."

"I'm house sitting. Out at the Aldridge place."

The scanner stops beeping.

The girl looks at me. Really looks, for the first time. Then her eyes flick past my shoulder toward the front door of the store, and I turn to see what she's looking at.

On the corkboard by the door, between an ad for firewood and a flyer for a church pancake breakfast, there's a poster. The paper is faded and curled at the corners, like it's been there a long time.

MISSING, it says across the top.

Below that, a photograph of a young woman with a wide smile and dark curly hair, squinting into the sun. She looks maybe twenty-four.

MADELINE "MADDIE" KERR. Age 24. Last seen October 14 at a residence on Lake Tamarack, where she was employed as a house sitter.

A house sitter.

On Lake Tamarack.

I look back at the cashier. She's scanning my groceries again, fast, not meeting my eyes.

"That residence," I say. "Which one was it?"

"Forty-two eighty," she mumbles.

I don't have to check. I know the address. I typed it into my GPS yesterday morning.

* * *

In the parking lot, I sit in my car with the engine running and the heat on full blast and my hands shaking on the wheel.

It's a coincidence. It has to be. Lake Tamarack has, what, a hundred houses on it? And the Aldridges are rich; rich people have staff; staff sometimes leave. Maybe Maddie Kerr ran off with a boyfriend. Maybe she's in Florida right now with a new name and a new life, laughing about the poster.

Someone knocks on my window, and I scream.

It's a man in a tan uniform. Sheriff's department. He holds up both hands, palms out, and I roll the window down with a trembling finger.

"Sorry," he says. "Didn't mean to scare you. You all right?"

"Fine. You just startled me."

He's around forty, with a kind, tired face and a gray-flecked mustache. His name tag says ORTEGA. "Jess in there says you're staying out at the Aldridge house."

Small towns. Of course.

"For six weeks," I say. "House sitting."

Deputy Ortega nods slowly. He glances toward the store, toward the poster I know he can see from here.

"Mind if I give you my card?" He's already holding it out. "Cell number's on the back. If anything out there feels off, you call me. Day or night."

"Off how?"

He hesitates. I can see him deciding how much to say.

"Big house, lot of land, a long way from anybody," he says finally. "I just like people to have a number to call."

"What happened to Maddie Kerr?"

His jaw tightens. "That's an open investigation, ma'am."

"But she worked for them. The Aldridges."

"She did." He taps the roof of my car twice, like he's ending the conversation. "Lock your doors at night, Ms.—?"

"Vance. Nora."

"Lock your doors, Nora."

He walks back to his cruiser. I watch him go. Then I do the thing I'd have told any client at my old law firm never to do.

I pull out my phone and search Maddie Kerr Lake Tamarack.

sections.title: Chapter 4
sections.html:
Chapter 4

Rule #7: If Grant calls your cell, do not answer.

The articles aren't long. Local news doesn't go in for long.

Madeline Kerr, twenty-four, of Duluth, was hired by Grant and Celeste Aldridge last September to house-sit their Lake Tamarack property while they traveled. On the evening of October 14, she spoke to her mother by phone and "seemed happy." On October 16, her mother reported her missing after she stopped answering texts. Her car was found three days later at a hiking trailhead twelve miles away, keys on the seat. Search teams walked the woods for a week. Divers checked the shallows near the trailhead.

Nothing.

One article, from a Duluth paper, includes a single paragraph that makes my skin go cold:

Authorities confirmed that Grant Aldridge, 44, a Minneapolis technology investor and the owner of the property, was interviewed multiple times. Sources close to the investigation say Aldridge was considered a person of interest. He has not been charged. His wife, Celeste Aldridge, told reporters the couple was "devastated" and "praying for Maddie's safe return."

A person of interest.

I think about rule seven. If Grant calls your cell, do not answer.

Maybe it isn't insane. Maybe it's the only rule that makes sense.

* * *

Back at the house, Juniper greets me at the door for the first time, tail wagging so hard her whole back half sways.

"Look at you," I say, scratching her ears. "Are we friends now?"

She trots away toward the mudroom, where her bed is, a big plaid cushion stuffed into a corner. She turns in three circles and flops down, and then she starts digging at the cushion with her front paws. Frantic. Whining.

"Hey. Hey, what's wrong?"

She keeps digging, until the zipper on the side of the cushion catches on a claw and pulls halfway open. Stuffing spills out. And with it, something small and pink.

A phone case.

It's cheap, rubbery, the kind you buy at a mall kiosk. There's no phone inside it. But tucked into the clear pocket on the back, where some people keep a credit card, there's a strip of photo-booth pictures.

Four frames. A girl with dark curly hair, laughing. A man beside her, older, handsome, with a jaw like a movie star and silver at his temples. In the first frame they're making silly faces. In the second, they're both laughing. In the third, he's looking at her instead of the camera.

In the fourth, they're kissing.

The girl is Maddie Kerr. I know that face now. I've seen it on a missing poster and in four different news articles.

And the man, I'm almost sure, is Grant Aldridge. I found his headshot on his company's website this afternoon. Same jaw. Same silver.

I sit down hard on the mudroom floor.

"Oh my God, Juniper," I whisper. "Did you hide this?"

The dog puts her head in my lap and sighs.

* * *

My phone rings at 6:14 p.m.

I'm chopping onions, and I nearly take off a finger. The number is unknown, a Minneapolis area code. I let it ring. After a minute, the voicemail notification pops up.

I shouldn't listen to it. I know that.

I listen to it.

"Nora. This is Grant Aldridge." A man's voice, deep, strained, like he's been talking too much or not sleeping. "I know what Celeste told you. I know about the rules. Please, you need to call me back, it's very important that you—"

The message cuts off. Not like he hung up. Like it just stopped.

I play it four times. Then I delete it, and I pull the list of rules off the fridge, and I read number seven over and over until the words don't look like words anymore.

At 7:00, I feed Juniper.

At 9:00, the landline rings.

"Say it," says Celeste.

My voice comes out steady. I'm proud of that. "All quiet."

I don't mention the phone case. I don't mention the voicemail. I don't know why. Maybe it's because the whole time I'm holding the phone, I have the strangest feeling that she already knows.

sections.title: Chapter 5
sections.html:
Chapter 5

Rule #5: The lights facing the lake stay on from dusk to dawn.

On my fourth morning at the lake, a canoe comes across the bay.

I'm on the deck with my coffee, bundled in a blanket, watching the mist burn off the water. The canoe glides out of the fog like something out of a ghost story: dark green, low in the water, one figure paddling slow and steady. It comes straight toward the Aldridge dock.

I stand up. Rule two runs through my head. Never let anyone inside. But this person isn't coming inside. This person is coming to the dock. Which is right beside the boathouse.

The canoe bumps against the pilings. An old man climbs out with surprising ease, ties off the line, and starts walking up the slope toward me. He's wearing a plaid wool coat, a knit cap, and the expression of someone who has been annoyed about something for approximately seventy years.

"You the new one?" he calls.

"I'm Nora. I'm house sitting."

"I know what you're doing." He stops at the bottom of the deck stairs and doesn't come up, which I appreciate. "Dell Harker. I'm across the bay. White house, red trim." He jerks a thumb over his shoulder. I can just make it out through the thinning mist, a small square house on the opposite shore, maybe half a mile away.

"Nice to meet you, Mr. Harker."

"Dell." He squints up at the house, at all that glass. "She give you the list?"

My stomach tightens. "What list?"

"Don't play dumb, it doesn't suit you. The rules. She had a list for the last girl too."

"Maddie."

He looks at me sharply. "So you've heard."

"I saw the poster in town."

Dell nods slowly. He pulls a pipe from his coat pocket, doesn't light it, just holds it. "Maddie used to wave at me from that dock every morning. Nice girl. Loud laugh. You could hear it across the water." He turns the pipe over in his fingers. "Last girl didn't follow the rules either. Or maybe she did. Hard to say which would've been worse."

"What does that mean?"

He's quiet for a long moment. Across the bay, a loon calls, that long, haunted sound that makes the hair stand up on your arms.

"Night of October fourteenth," he says. "I don't sleep much. Old man thing. I was on my porch around two in the morning, and there was a light on in that boathouse." He points with the pipe stem. "Nobody uses that boathouse. Hasn't been a boat in it since the Aldridges bought the place. But there was a light. And then there wasn't."

The coffee in my stomach turns sour. "Did you tell the police?"

Dell's mouth twists. "I told them. Deputy wrote it down. But I'd had a few that night, and I'm the crazy old coot who's been in a property line fight with the Aldridges for three years. So." He shrugs. "They checked the boathouse. Said it was empty."

"Then maybe it was empty."

"Maybe." He puts the pipe back in his pocket and turns toward his canoe. Then he stops. "Your lights."

"What?"

"The ones facing the lake. You keep 'em on all night?"

"It's one of the rules."

"Huh." He looks out across the bay, toward his own small house. "Maddie did too. Every night. Like a lighthouse." He starts walking. "Makes you wonder who's supposed to be watching."

* * *

I think about that all day.

Rule five says the lights stay on from dusk to dawn. I'd assumed it was about security, some rich-person thing about deterring burglars. But Dell's right. With the lights on, the house becomes a glass box on a hill. Anybody across the bay with a decent pair of binoculars could watch every move I make.

Anybody. Including Dell.

That night, after the nine o'clock call, I stand in the dark of my bedroom and look out across the water, at the small white house with the red trim. There's a light in one of the windows.

As I watch, it goes out.

And a second later, one of the lake-facing lights on the Aldridge deck, directly below my window, goes out too.

sections.title: Chapter 6
sections.html:
Chapter 6

Rule #2: Never let anyone inside. No matter who they say they are.

It's just a bulb.

I tell myself this as I stand frozen at the window. Bulbs burn out. It's the most normal thing in the world. The timing is a coincidence. Of course it is.

But rule five says the lights stay on from dusk to dawn, and I have a strange, crawling certainty that if I don't fix it, Celeste will know.

I find a flashlight in the kitchen drawer and a box of bulbs in the mudroom closet. Juniper follows me to the back door and then stops, and won't come any farther, and just stands there with her ears flat, whining softly.

"Stay," I tell her. As if she had any intention of going.

Outside, the cold hits like a slap. It's maybe thirty-five degrees, the air sharp with pine and something muddier underneath, the smell of the lake. The deck wraps around the back of the house, and the dead light is at the far corner, a black fixture mounted on a post by the stairs that lead down toward the water.

I unscrew the bulb. It's hot. Scalding hot. I yelp and drop it, and it shatters on the deck boards.

It wasn't burned out, then. Bulbs that burn out go cold.

Someone switched it off. Or unscrewed it just enough to break the connection.

I screw in the new bulb with trembling fingers, and light floods the deck again, spilling down the slope toward the dock. And that's when I see it.

A figure. Standing at the end of the dock, right beside the boathouse. Tall. Dark coat. Perfectly still. Facing the house.

Facing me.

I don't move. I can't. My whole body has turned to ice. The figure doesn't move either. We stand there, the two of us, two hundred feet apart, and I think: He can see me. I'm standing in a pool of light like an actor on a stage, and he can see everything.

Then the figure turns, steps off the edge of the dock, and is gone.

Not into the water. I'd have heard a splash. Into the shadow beside the boathouse, where the light doesn't reach.

I run.

I'm through the back door and slamming the deadbolt before I even know I've moved. I set the alarm with fingers that keep missing the buttons. Juniper is barking now, deep, frantic barks, standing in the middle of the kitchen with her hackles up.

I grab my phone and Deputy Ortega's card and dial.

"Ortega."

"This is Nora Vance, at the Aldridge house. There's someone here. On the dock. By the boathouse."

His voice changes instantly, all the sleep draining out of it. "Are they trying to get inside?"

"No, I don't think so, they just, they were standing there. Watching."

"Stay inside. Keep your doors locked. I'm twenty minutes out."

* * *

It takes him twenty-six minutes. I count every one of them.

I watch his flashlight beam bob down the slope, sweep the dock, circle the boathouse. He rattles the padlock. He walks the shoreline in both directions. After fifteen minutes, he climbs back up to the deck, and I unlock the door for him.

"Nobody there now," he says. "But somebody was. There's fresh mud on the dock boards. Boot prints. Men's size, I'd guess. Heading along the shore toward the road."

"Could it have been Dell Harker? From across the bay?"

Ortega raises his eyebrows. "Dell's seventy-six and has two bad knees. I'd be surprised if he could get up that slope." He looks at me more carefully. "Why would you think it was Dell?"

"I don't know. He came by this morning. He said some things about Maddie."

Something closes in Ortega's face. "Dell says a lot of things." He zips his jacket. "I'll take a look around the road in the morning. You call me if they come back."

After he leaves, I don't go to bed. I sit on the living room couch with Juniper pressed against my leg and every light in the house blazing, and I watch the dark water.

At some point, I must fall asleep. Because the next thing I know, it's past midnight, and someone is knocking on the front door.

sections.title: Chapter 7
sections.html:
Chapter 7

Rule #2: Never let anyone inside. No matter who they say they are.

Three knocks. Slow. Heavy.

Juniper is already on her feet, rigid, staring at the front hall. She isn't barking. Somehow that's worse.

I get up. I don't want to. My legs carry me into the entryway anyway, into the long hall where the front door stands, a slab of solid oak with a narrow window of frosted glass beside it. Through the glass I can see a shape. A man. Tall.

Three more knocks.

"Nora?" His voice is muffled through the wood. Deep. Familiar. "Nora, I know you're in there. Please. I just need to talk to you."

I know that voice. I've listened to it four times on a voicemail.

"It's Grant," he says. "Grant Aldridge. This is my house. Please open the door."

Never let anyone inside. No matter who they say they are.

"I can't," I say. My voice cracks. "I'm sorry. I'm not supposed to let anyone in."

"I know. I know what she told you." He sounds exhausted, desperate. "Listen to me. Celeste isn't in Portugal. She was never going to Portugal. Whatever she's told you about me, about the rules, you can't trust it. You need to get out of this house."

"You're a person of interest," I say, "in a missing persons case."

A long silence on the other side of the door.

"Yes," he says quietly. "I am. And I didn't do it. But I think I know who did, and I think you're in danger, and I'm asking you, please—"

"I'm calling the police."

"Nora—"

"I have a deputy's number. He'll be here in twenty minutes."

Another silence. Then, so low I almost don't hear it: "Ask her about the third floor."

The shape behind the glass moves away. I hear footsteps on the porch, then gravel, then nothing.

I dial Ortega with shaking hands. It goes to voicemail. I leave a message, babbling, and then I sit on the floor of the front hall with my back against the wall, and Juniper lies down beside me, and neither of us moves until the sky outside the frosted glass turns gray.

When I finally open the door at dawn, there's something on the welcome mat.

A single key. Old, brass, heavy. Tied to it with a piece of red string is a paper tag, and on the tag, in blocky handwriting, someone has written one word.

UPSTAIRS.

sections.title: Chapter 8
sections.html:
Chapter 8

Rule #4: The third floor is closed. Don't go up.

Ortega calls back at eight in the morning, apologizing. He was on a car wreck out on Highway 1 until three a.m.

"He said he was Grant Aldridge," I tell him. "He said Celeste isn't in Portugal."

A pause on the line. "Did you let him in?"

"No."

"Good." I hear him exhale. "Nora, I'm going to be straight with you, because I think you deserve it. Grant Aldridge hasn't been charged with anything. It's his house. Legally, he's allowed to knock on his own front door."

"He's a suspect."

"He's a person of interest. That's not the same thing." Ortega sounds tired, and not just from the car wreck. "If he threatens you, if he tries to force his way in, that's different. Then you call me and I come, and I do something about it. But right now, all I've got is a man who wanted to talk to his house sitter."

I don't tell him about the key.

I don't know why. It's sitting in the pocket of my jeans, heavy as a stone, and every time I shift my weight I feel it against my thigh. UPSTAIRS. Maybe I don't tell him because I know exactly what he'd say. Don't go up there, Nora. Give it to me. And some small, stupid, curious part of me isn't ready to give it up.

* * *

I spend the day not going upstairs.

I clean the kitchen, which is already clean. I take Juniper on a long walk down the gravel drive and back. I sit on the deck with my laptop and apply for eleven jobs I won't get. Twice, I find myself standing at the bottom of the staircase to the third floor, staring up at that dark door, and twice I turn around and walk away.

At noon, my phone buzzes with a notification from my bank. A deposit of $3,000.00 has been made to your account.

The first half of my payment. Right on schedule.

Four minutes later, a debt collector calls about my credit card. For the first time in months, I answer. I pay the full past-due balance while the woman on the phone is still reading me her script, and when she says, "Oh, well, thank you, Ms. Vance," in a surprised voice, I almost cry.

This is why I'm here. This is why I'm going to follow the rules.

Three thousand dollars more when the job is done. Five more weeks. That's all.

* * *

At nine o'clock, the landline rings.

"Say it."

"All quiet," I say. And then, before she can hang up: "Celeste. Wait."

Silence. But she hasn't hung up. I can hear her breathing. I can hear something else too, a faint background hum, like a refrigerator or a fan.

"Grant came to the house last night," I say.

"Did you open the door?"

"No."

"Good girl." The words make my skin crawl. "Grant isn't well, Nora. We're separating. He's been saying things he shouldn't. Whatever he told you, ignore it."

"He said you're not in Portugal."

A soft laugh. "Where else would I be?"

It isn't an answer. We both know it isn't an answer.

"He told me," I say carefully, "to ask you about the third floor."

The silence this time is different. Longer. Colder. When she speaks again, her voice has changed. It's still calm, still even, but underneath it there's something hard, like ice under snow.

"And what," Celeste says, "would make you want to ask me that?"

My hand goes to my pocket. To the key.

"Nothing," I say. "Just curious."

"Curiosity isn't in the rules, Nora."

The line goes dead.

sections.title: Chapter 9
sections.html:
Chapter 9

Rule #8: Burn nothing in the fireplace.

I was seventeen, and my sister Ivy was fifteen, and it was the hottest day of the summer.

There was a quarry outside our town, an old granite pit that had filled with rainwater decades ago. Everybody knew you weren't supposed to swim there. There were signs, and a chain-link fence with a hole in it big enough to drive a car through. Every summer, some kid from the high school cracked his head on a submerged ledge, and every summer, everybody kept going anyway.

Ivy wanted to jump from the high rock. Forty feet. The seniors did it. She wanted to be a senior so badly it made her reckless.

I told her not to.

That's what I told the police afterward, and it's true. I told her not to. I said, Ivy, you'll break your neck. I said, Mom will kill us both. I said a lot of things.

What I didn't tell the police is that we'd been fighting all week. About a boy, of course. About a stupid boy with a stupid truck whose name I can't even remember now. I didn't tell them that when Ivy jumped, and hit the water wrong, and came up sputtering and then went under again, I stood on that rock and I didn't move.

I counted.

I don't know why I counted. Maybe my brain needed something to do while the rest of me froze. One. Two. Three. I watched the ripples spreading out from where she'd gone under, and I counted, and somewhere around twenty I understood that she wasn't coming back up on her own.

At thirty, I jumped.

They told me afterward it probably wouldn't have mattered. That she'd likely hit her head on the way in. That thirty seconds wouldn't have made a difference.

I've never believed them.

* * *

I don't sleep that night. I lie in bed with the key in my fist, thinking about Ivy and about Maddie Kerr, two girls who went into the dark and didn't come back, and about the voice on the phone saying Curiosity isn't in the rules.

At three in the morning, I get up.

I don't turn on any lights. Juniper lifts her head from the rug at the foot of my bed and watches me go, but she doesn't follow.

The hallway is dark, silver moonlight falling through the windows. The staircase to the third floor is darker. I climb it slowly, one hand on the wall, counting the steps without meaning to. Fourteen of them.

At the top, the door. Dark wood. Brass deadbolt.

I fit the key into the lock. It turns so smoothly it's like the lock has been waiting for me.

sections.title: Chapter 10
sections.html:
Chapter 10

Rule #4: The third floor is closed. Don't go up.

The first thing I notice is the hum.

It's the same sound I heard on the phone. Low, electrical, constant. The sound of machines.

The second thing I notice is the light: blue, cold, flickering, coming from the far end of a long, low room under the slope of the roof.

I find a switch by the door and flip it. Nothing happens. Then I see the tiny red light on the switch plate, and understand that it's not a light switch. It's a sensor.

Somewhere, some device has just recorded that this door opened.

I should run. I know I should run. Instead, I walk toward the blue light.

It's a desk. A long, sleek desk against the far wall, and on the desk there are six monitors arranged in two rows of three, and on each monitor there's a grid of tiny video feeds, black and white, grainy, night vision.

The kitchen. The living room, where the fireplace is. The front hall. The mudroom, where Juniper's torn bed still sits in the corner. The deck. The dock. The driveway. The long second-floor hallway.

My bedroom.

I stare at it. In the grainy feed, I can see my bed, the blankets thrown back where I got out of it. I can see Juniper on the rug, her head on her paws, her eyes glinting white in the infrared. I can see the chair where I tossed my clothes. The window. The door.

Every night. Every night I've been in this house, someone has been able to watch me sleep.

I think of the nine o'clock calls. Say it. I think of the light on the deck going out. I think of Celeste's voice when I asked about the third floor, the way she already sounded like she knew.

She did know. She's always known. She's been watching me the whole time.

* * *

There's a keyboard in front of the monitors. A mouse. I touch it, and one of the screens jumps to a desktop with a single folder on it, labeled ARCHIVE.

Inside ARCHIVE, there are dozens of video files, each named with a date. I scroll. The files go back almost two years. And there, in the middle of the list:

10-14.mp4

I click it before I can stop myself.

It's the kitchen feed. Night, the timestamp in the corner reading 11:41 PM. The room is lit only by the light over the stove. A young woman walks into the frame. Dark curly hair, a sweatshirt too big for her, bare feet.

Maddie.

She goes to the fridge, gets out a bottle of water, and turns, and freezes. She's looking at someone just off camera. Someone standing in the doorway to the living room.

There's no sound. But I can see her mouth moving. I can see her face going from surprised, to scared, to angry. She points at the ceiling. Up. Toward this room. Toward where I'm standing now.

She says something, and it's short, and I lean closer to the monitor, and I watch her lips, and I'm almost sure it's: I'll tell him what you did.

Then she takes a step toward the doorway. Toward whoever is standing there.

And the screen goes black.

I stare at it. I click the file again. It plays to the same point, the same step, the same black screen. The file ends there. Six more seconds of timestamp, and nothing.

Somebody cut it.

With shaking fingers, I scroll to the bottom of the ARCHIVE list. The most recent files. They have this month's dates.

The last one is today's. It's still recording. When I click it, a live feed opens: the third-floor hallway. The camera is mounted above the door I just came through.

On the screen, a woman stands at a desk with her back to the camera, staring at a monitor.

Me.

Somewhere downstairs, in the silent house, the landline starts to ring.

sections.title: Chapter 11
sections.html:
Chapter 11

Rule #3: The landline will ring at nine every night. Answer it.

It's 3:22 in the morning.

The landline rings and rings, and I can hear it from the third floor, echoing up the stairwell, shrill and impossible. I could ignore it. I could lock the door behind me and pack my bag and drive away and never come back.

But she'd know. She knows everything.

I walk down the stairs. Down the second-floor hall. Down to the kitchen. I don't turn on the lights. The phone keeps ringing, twelve rings, fifteen, twenty. It doesn't stop. Whoever's calling will let it ring forever.

I pick it up.

"You went upstairs," Celeste says.

I don't answer.

"I wondered how long you'd last. Maddie made it nineteen days." A small, satisfied sound. "You made it six. I'm impressed. Or disappointed. I haven't decided."

"You've been watching me."

"It's my house, Nora. I watch everything in my house." There's that hum again, behind her voice. Wherever she is, she's surrounded by machines too. "Don't be dramatic. You'd do the same if you had nice things."

"Where is Maddie Kerr?"

"Maddie didn't follow the rules."

Just like that. Flat and simple, the way you'd say the milk went bad.

"I'm calling the police," I say.

"Are you?" She sounds genuinely curious. "And what will you tell them? That you trespassed into a locked room in a house you were hired to protect? That you watched a video that shows a girl getting a bottle of water? Deputy Ortega is a nice man, Nora. He's also very tired, and he's already spent a year chasing ghosts on this lake."

"The video was cut. Somebody cut it."

"Files corrupt all the time." A pause. "And while you're talking to Deputy Ortega, perhaps you could explain Mrs. Patterson of Edina."

My whole body goes cold.

"Mrs. Patterson," Celeste continues pleasantly, "who doesn't exist. Whose phone number belongs to a Natasha Greer of Northeast Minneapolis. Your roommate, I believe. You lied on your application, Nora. You committed fraud to get into my house. I have the emails. I have the recording of the reference call. I record all my calls."

"That's not—"

"And then," she says, softer now, almost gentle, "there's Ivy."

I can't breathe.

"I did my research. I always do. The Hennepin County Sheriff's report is public, did you know that? Witness states she observed the victim struggling in the water for approximately thirty seconds before entering the water herself. Thirty seconds, Nora. That's a long time to stand still and watch your sister drown."

"Stop."

"I'm not judging you. Truly. I think we understand each other better than you'd like." The hum on the line grows louder, then fades, like she's walking through a room. "So here's what's going to happen. You're going to go back to bed. You're going to follow the rules for three more weeks. And then I'm going to pay you the rest of your money, and you're going to drive away and forget all about my house. Or."

"Or what?"

"Or you can try to tell someone. And I'll tell them about Mrs. Patterson. And about Ivy. And about the way you've been snooping through my private files at three in the morning. And then we'll see who they believe. The rich, grieving wife of a man who was once suspected of something terrible? Or the unemployed liar with a dead sister and a long history of bad decisions?"

I don't say anything. I can't.

"Go to bed, Nora," Celeste says. "And lock the third floor behind you. Rule four."

Click.

sections.title: Chapter 12
sections.html:
Chapter 12

Rule #9: Never go to the boathouse.

I pack in eleven minutes.

I don't care about the three thousand dollars anymore. I don't care about the rules or the fraud or the Hennepin County Sheriff's report. I throw everything I own into my duffel bag and I clip Juniper's leash to her collar, because I'm not leaving her in this house, not for one more night. And I walk out the front door into the gray pre-dawn cold and I get into my car.

I turn the key.

Nothing.

Not a click, not a cough. Dead.

I try again. And again. I pop the hood and get out and stand there staring at the engine like I have any idea what I'm looking at. But even I can see it. The thick black cable that runs to the battery has been cut. A clean slice, right through the rubber and the copper, the two ends hanging a few inches apart.

I look up at the house. At all those windows. At the tiny black dome of a camera tucked under the eave above the garage, which I've walked past every day for a week without seeing.

She did this. Or someone did it for her. While I was asleep. While I was on the third floor.

My phone has one bar. I call Ortega. Voicemail. I call again. Voicemail. I text him: Please call me. It's urgent. Aldridge house. I text Tasha: If you don't hear from me by tonight, call the Pell County sheriff. The text sits there with a little spinning wheel beside it, refusing to send.

The house Wi-Fi. I could connect to the house Wi-Fi.

Which she controls.

I stand in the driveway with Juniper pressed against my leg, both of us shivering, and I look out across the lake. The mist is lifting. On the far shore, half a mile away, I can see the small white house with the red trim.

Dell Harker.

The only other person on this lake who seems to know something is wrong.

"Come on," I tell Juniper. "We're going for a walk."

* * *

It's two miles around the south end of the bay by the road. I walk it fast, Juniper trotting beside me, my duffel bag banging against my hip. Every time a car passes, I flinch. Only two do: a pickup full of firewood and a mail truck. Neither slows down.

Dell's house is small and neat and badly in need of paint. There's no car in the gravel driveway. I knock on the front door and nobody answers.

"Dell?" I call. "It's Nora. From the Aldridge house."

Nothing. The windows are dark.

I walk around the side. The backyard slopes down to the water, where his green canoe sits overturned on a pair of sawhorses. Beside it, there's a shed, a little wooden thing with a single dusty window. The door is ajar.

I shouldn't go in. I know I shouldn't go in.

But I've already broken rule four. What's one more?

sections.title: Chapter 13
sections.html:
Chapter 13

Rule #6: No photos of the house. Not online. Not anywhere.

The shed smells like motor oil and old paper.

There's a workbench along one wall, cluttered with fishing tackle and coffee cans full of screws. There's a lawnmower, a rake, a pair of oars. And by the single window, which looks straight out across the bay, there's a wooden stool, and a tripod, and on the tripod, a pair of binoculars the size of a small child.

I bend down and put my eye to them.

The Aldridge house leaps into view, so close I gasp. I can see the deck. I can see the light fixture I replaced. I can see the window of my own bedroom, the curtains I never close. I can even see the blue flicker of the monitors through the small, high window of the third floor.

I pull back, heart racing.

Stacked on the workbench beside the tripod are notebooks. Dozens of them. Spiral-bound, the cheap kind you buy for school. I pick up the one on top and open it.

Dates. Times. Tiny, cramped handwriting.

Oct 3. 7:02 AM. New girl on deck w/ coffee. Dog out.

Oct 3. 9:00 PM. Kitchen light. On phone. 30 sec.

Oct 5. 11:47 PM. Deck light out. Girl outside w/ flashlight. Figure on dock. Man, tall. Gone 11:49.

It's me. He's been writing down everything I do.

I flip back. Further. Months of entries. Years. The house, the lights, the cars coming and going. And then I find the notebook with last October on the cover, and my fingers go numb as I turn the pages.

Oct 14. 11:40 PM. Maddie in kitchen. Someone else there.

Oct 14. 11:52 PM. Kitchen dark.

Oct 15. 2:10 AM. Light in boathouse.

Oct 15. 2:31 AM. Rowboat out from boathouse. One person rowing. Heavy load, low in water. Toward the deep hole by the point.

Oct 15. 2:58 AM. Rowboat back. Light off.

And below that, underlined twice, pressed so hard into the paper that the pen tore through:

C.A. Not G. It was HER.

Behind me, the shed door creaks open.

I spin around. Dell Harker is standing in the doorway, and he's holding a shotgun.

"Well," he says. "I guess you've met my hobby."

sections.title: Chapter 14
sections.html:
Chapter 14

Rule #2: Never let anyone inside.

For a long, awful second, neither of us moves.

Then Dell looks down at the shotgun in his hands like he's just noticed it, and sighs, and props it against the doorframe. "Thought you were a raccoon," he says. "Raccoons have been getting into my feed."

"You've been watching me." My voice is shaking. "You've been watching everything."

"I've been watching that house." He jerks his head toward the window. "Not you. Whoever's in it. There's a difference."

"Is there?"

Dell doesn't answer right away. He lowers himself onto an overturned bucket with a groan, rubbing his knee. Up close, in the gray light from the window, he looks older than he did on the dock. Tired. His hands are shaking a little.

"My wife, Ruth," he says. "She passed three years ago. Cancer. Before she died, the Aldridges bought that place, tore down the old cabin, put up that glass monstrosity. Ruth met Celeste exactly once. At the post office. Came home and said to me, Dell, that woman's not right. There's nothing behind her eyes." He shakes his head. "Ruth was a nurse for forty years. She knew people."

"So you started watching."

"I started watching." He shrugs. "Old man, no wife, can't sleep. Better than television."

I hold up the notebook. "You saw her. That night. With Maddie."

Dell's face goes very still.

"You told the police there was a light in the boathouse," I say. "But you didn't tell them this. That you saw her rowing out. That it was Celeste, not Grant."

"I told them." His voice is low and rough. "I told them all of it. Deputy wrote it down. Then two days later, a lawyer from Minneapolis shows up at my door with a folder. Pictures of me at the Tamarack Tap that night. Receipts. Six whiskeys. And a letter about my property line dispute, and a whole lot of words about harassment and defamation and how an old drunk with a grudge against his neighbors wasn't a reliable witness to anything."

"And the police believed her."

"The police believed what they could prove. Which was nothing." He looks out the window at the house. "They searched the boathouse, like I said. It was empty. Clean as a whistle. And there's a spot out by the point, where that rowboat went, where the lake drops off to ninety feet. Coldest, darkest water in the county. Divers won't go that deep without a good reason and a lot of money."

I sink down onto the stool by the binoculars. My legs won't hold me anymore.

"She knows," I say. "She knows I went upstairs. She's got cameras everywhere. She cut my battery cable. And she knows things about me. Things I've never told anyone." I hear my voice crack. "She said if I tell anyone, she'll make sure nobody believes me."

Dell nods slowly, like none of this surprises him.

"That's what she does," he says. "She finds out what you're ashamed of, and she makes it into a leash."

sections.title: Chapter 15
sections.html:
Chapter 15

Rule #7: If Grant calls your cell, do not answer.

Dell drives me into Pell in a pickup truck older than I am, with Juniper wedged between us on the bench seat. He drops me at the Loon Café, the only place in town with public Wi-Fi, and says he'll go find Ortega himself.

"Man's either at the station or at the Tap," he says. "Either way, I know where to look."

I order a coffee I don't want and connect to the Wi-Fi. My texts finally go through, all of them at once. Tasha replies within thirty seconds: WHAT?? are you ok?? do I call someone?? I type back that I'm okay for now, that I'm in town, that I'll explain later.

Then my phone rings. The Minneapolis number.

Rule seven.

I answer it.

"Nora." Grant Aldridge sounds like he hasn't slept in a week. "Thank God. Where are you?"

"Where are you?"

A pause. Then: "Look out the window."

I look. Across the street, in the parking lot of the Lutheran church, there's a dusty silver sedan. The driver's door opens, and a man steps out. Tall. Dark coat. Silver at his temples.

He raises one hand. Not waving. Just showing me he's there.

"I'm not going to come in unless you want me to," he says in my ear. "I'm not going to come any closer. But I'd like to talk to you. Five minutes. In a public place, with people around. And then you can decide for yourself."

I look at the handful of people in the café. An old couple sharing a cinnamon roll. A guy in hunting camo on his laptop. The waitress, who's been reading the same magazine for twenty minutes.

"Five minutes," I say.

* * *

Up close, Grant Aldridge looks less like a movie star and more like a man who's been drowning for a year. His eyes are bloodshot. There's a cut on his knuckle, half healed. When the waitress brings him coffee, he wraps both hands around the mug like it's the only warm thing left in the world.

"Did you use the key?" he asks.

"Yes."

He closes his eyes. "Then you saw."

"I saw cameras. I saw a video of Maddie in the kitchen, and it cuts off right when she walks toward someone." I lean forward. "Was it you?"

"No." He opens his eyes and looks straight at me. "I was in Minneapolis that night. At a dinner with forty people. The police confirmed it."

"Then why are you a person of interest?"

He reaches into his coat and slides his phone across the table to me. On the screen is a text message thread. The contact name is just M.

The last message was sent at 11:48 p.m. on October 14.

C knows. She's here. Come now please.

"I didn't see it until six in the morning," he says quietly. "I'd turned my phone off at the dinner. By the time I got to the lake, Maddie was gone. And the police found this text, and they found out about the affair, and suddenly the husband with the secret girlfriend was their favorite story. They think I drove up that night. They think she threatened to tell my wife, and I panicked." He laughs, a terrible hollow sound. "Celeste already knew. Celeste always knows. She's the one who hired Maddie, Nora. Personally. Out of all the applicants. Young, pretty, broke, alone. I think she chose her on purpose. I think she wanted to watch what I'd do."

My coffee has gone cold. "Why are you telling me this?"

"Because the house is hers. The money is hers. There's a prenup that would leave me with nothing, and a year of rumors that have left me with less than nothing. Nobody will listen to me." He leans forward. "But Maddie's phone was never found. And I think it's still in that house. I think Celeste kept it, the way she keeps everything. And I think she's planning to use it."

"Use it how?"

"To finish what the police started," Grant says. "To make sure someone finds it in the right place, at the right time. With my fingerprints on it."

He looks at me across the table, and his eyes are wet.

"And I think she hired you," he says, "to be the one who finds it."

sections.title: Chapter 16
sections.html:
Chapter 16

Rule #5: The lights facing the lake stay on from dusk to dawn.

Dell comes back with Ortega twenty minutes later.

The deputy's face goes through several expressions when he sees Grant Aldridge sitting across from me in a booth at the Loon Café. None of them are happy. But he slides in beside me without a word, and he listens. He listens to all of it. The cameras, the key, the cut video, the phone call at three in the morning. He reads Dell's notebook page from October fourteenth twice, his thumb resting on the words It was HER.

When I get to the part about Mrs. Patterson of Edina, I make myself say it plainly. That I lied. That my roommate faked my reference. I wait for him to look at me the way Celeste said everyone would.

He just nods and writes something down.

"Here's what I can tell you," Ortega says finally. He keeps his voice low. "After you called me the other night, I ran Celeste Aldridge through a few databases. She didn't board an international flight out of MSP this month. Or out of Duluth. Or out of Chicago." He glances at Grant. "Neither did you."

"I told you," Grant says. "I never went. She told me she was going alone."

"So where is she?" I ask.

"I don't know." Ortega looks out the café window, toward the lake you can't see from here. "But I don't think she's far."

"Then arrest her," Dell says.

"For what? Lying about a vacation? Putting cameras in her own house?" Ortega rubs his face. "I believe you, Dell. I think I believed you last year, too, and I let a lawyer from Minneapolis talk me out of it, and I'm going to have to live with that. But believing isn't evidence. That spot by the point is ninety feet deep. To get the state dive team in there, I need something solid. Something a judge can hold in his hand."

"Maddie's phone," Grant says.

Everyone looks at him.

"It's in the house," he says. "I'd bet my life on it. Celeste doesn't throw things away. She keeps them. She files them. She uses them."

Ortega is quiet for a long moment. Then he turns to me. "If you go back there, I can't protect you. I'm one deputy covering four hundred square miles. I'd tell you not to go."

"If I don't go back," I say, "she'll know something's wrong. And she'll get rid of it."

We look at each other.

"Thirty seconds," I say, and nobody at the table knows what I mean except me. "I've been standing still for thirty seconds for fourteen years. I'm not doing it again."

* * *

Grant splices my battery cable in the Aldridge driveway with a kit from the hardware store, his hands quick and sure. He doesn't come inside. He doesn't even look at the house.

Ortega gives me a code. "You text me two words," he says. "All quiet. Anytime but nine o'clock. I'll know it means the opposite, and I'll send everybody I've got."

Dell gives me a canister of bear spray and tells me to aim for the eyes.

And then they leave, and I'm alone again, standing in front of the house with Juniper at my side and the sun going down behind the trees, and I walk inside and turn on every light that faces the lake.

Rule five. Let her watch.

sections.title: Chapter 17
sections.html:
Chapter 17

Rule #8: Burn nothing in the fireplace.

I act normal.

It's harder than it sounds, when you know there's an eye in every corner. I make dinner. I eat it at the island. I wash the plate. I sit on the couch with a book I don't read and scratch Juniper's ears and try to move like a woman who has nothing to hide, and every second I feel the cameras on my skin like cold fingers.

At nine, the phone rings.

"Say it."

"All quiet."

"You took a walk today." Celeste's voice is light. Almost amused. "All the way around the bay. And then you came back in Dell Harker's truck. I didn't know you two were friends."

"My car wouldn't start," I say evenly. "Somebody cut the battery cable."

"How awful. These back roads are full of vandals." A pause. "I've decided to come home early. Saturday. You'll be paid in full, of course. And then you can go."

Saturday. Four days.

"That's generous," I say.

"I'm a generous person." The hum on the line again. "Good night, Nora."

* * *

I lie awake thinking about where a person like Celeste would hide something.

Not somewhere random. Somewhere safe. Somewhere she controlled. And she controls this house with rules. Every rule is a fence. Don't open the door. Don't go upstairs. Don't go to the boathouse. Don't burn anything in the fireplace.

Why that one? It's such a strange rule. The fireplace is the centerpiece of the whole house, a column of stacked stone rising two stories. There's firewood stacked beside it. Matches on the mantel. Everything about it says light me. So why forbid it?

Unless there's something in there she doesn't want burned.

I get up at six, the way I always do, and let Juniper out, and make coffee. Then I get a bucket and a rag and a bottle of glass cleaner from the mudroom, and I go to the fireplace, and I start cleaning the glass doors.

It's the most boring thing in the world to watch. I hope.

I open the doors. I wipe the inside of the glass. I crouch down, like I'm scrubbing the back of the firebox. The camera in the living room is mounted high in the corner across the room. From that angle, it can see my back, my bent shoulders. It can't see my right hand reaching up into the dark throat of the chimney, past the open damper, feeling along the cold stone.

Soot. Grit. A spiderweb that makes me want to scream.

And then, on the smoke shelf, just above the damper, where nobody would ever look unless they were looking: plastic.

A freezer bag. Zipped shut. Something heavy inside.

My heart is beating so loudly I'm sure the camera can hear it. I pull the bag down slowly, and hold it against my stomach, below the edge of the firebox where it's hidden by my body, and I look.

A phone in a sparkly purple case. The screen is cracked in one corner.

And a man's leather glove. Brown, expensive, the kind with a little brand label stitched at the wrist.

Across the room, in the kitchen, the landline starts to ring.

It's 6:23 in the morning.

sections.title: Chapter 18
sections.html:
Chapter 18

Rule #3: Answer it.

I don't answer it.

I let it ring while I tuck the bag into the waistband of my leggings, under my big sweater. I let it ring while I close the fireplace doors and pick up my bucket and walk, slowly, slowly, into the kitchen. It rings twenty times. Thirty. It stops. It starts again.

I walk past it, into the pantry, and shut the door.

The pantry is the only room in the house I'm sure has no camera. I checked the feeds on the third floor. Kitchen, living room, halls, bedrooms, mudroom, deck, dock, driveway. No pantry. Even Celeste Aldridge draws the line at watching her canned tomatoes.

I sit on the floor between the shelves in the dark and take out the phone.

It's dead, of course. It's been dead for a year. But it's an iPhone, the same kind as mine, and my charger is in my back pocket, and there's an outlet by the floor where a little robot vacuum docks. I plug it in. I wait.

The landline stops ringing.

After three minutes, an apple glows white on the cracked screen. And then the lock screen.

The wallpaper is a photo of Maddie Kerr sitting on the Aldridge dock in a sundress, her arms around Juniper, both of them squinting into the sun. Juniper's muzzle is less gray. Maddie is laughing so hard her eyes are closed.

Below the photo, stacked like a gravestone, are the notifications that came in before the battery died.

G: I'm coming. Where are you? 6:14 AM

G: Maddie please answer 6:31 AM

Mom: Hi honey! Call me when you're up, love you 8:02 AM

Mom: Mads? 4:45 PM

Mom: Maddie please call me I'm getting worried 11:12 PM

I press my hand over my mouth and cry without making a sound.

* * *

I text Ortega on my own phone, fast, thumbs shaking. Found it. Chimney. Her phone + a man's glove.

He answers in less than a minute. Don't move it again. Don't let her know. I'm in Duluth for a court hearing until 5. I'll come at first light tomorrow. End of your drive, 6 AM. Can you hold on till then?

Yes, I type. It's one more night. I can do one more night.

I put the phone back in the bag and the bag back in my waistband, and I come out of the pantry with a can of soup in my hand, like that's what I went in for.

Then I go back to the third floor.

I don't care if she sees me. I need to look at the feeds. I need to understand the one thing that's been bothering me since I talked to Dell. He said he saw a rowboat go out from the boathouse on the night Maddie died. But the police searched the boathouse and found it empty.

Clean as a whistle, Dell said.

Too clean. Like someone had gone to the trouble to make it so.

On the monitor, I flip through the camera views until I find the dock camera. It points down the length of the dock, toward the water. You can see the side of the boathouse in the corner of the frame. The green door, the padlock.

And on the ground in front of that door, in last night's footage, something I missed before: a wheelbarrow that wasn't there when I arrived.

I play it back. 1:13 a.m. A figure in a long dark coat and a knit hat pushes the wheelbarrow down the path. The load is covered with a tarp. The figure unlocks the boathouse, wheels it inside, and comes back out with the wheelbarrow empty.

The face is turned away from the camera the whole time. On purpose.

But I don't need to see her face. I recognize the walk. I watched her walk to her Range Rover on my first day here.

Celeste was on this property last night. While I was sleeping. And she brought something to the boathouse.

sections.title: Chapter 19
sections.html:
Chapter 19

Rule #9: Never go to the boathouse.

I wait until two in the morning.

I don't know why two. Maybe because that's when Dell saw the light. Maybe because I want the dark to be as deep as it's going to get. I put on Grant's old barn coat from the mudroom and stick Dell's bear spray in one pocket and my phone in the other. I find bolt cutters in the garage, hanging on a pegboard beside the snow shovels.

Juniper follows me to the back door and whines.

"Stay," I tell her. "Guard the house."

She lies down in the doorway with her chin on her paws and watches me go.

* * *

The path down to the water is steep and slick with frost. The lake-facing lights throw long shadows across the slope, and past the edge of the light, everything is ink. I can hear the water before I reach it. Little waves slapping the pilings. The dock creaking under its own weight.

I hate water. I've hated it for fourteen years. I haven't been in a lake, a pool, the ocean, not even a hot tub. I shower fast with my eyes open. And now I'm walking toward the darkest water I've ever seen, in the middle of the night, carrying bolt cutters.

At the boathouse door, my hands are shaking so badly I have to try three times to get the jaws of the cutters around the padlock. Then I lean on them with all my weight, and the shackle snaps with a crack that echoes across the whole lake.

I freeze. Count. One, two, three.

Nothing moves. Across the bay, there's a single light on in Dell's house. I hope he's watching. For once, I hope someone is.

I open the door.

* * *

The smell hits me first. Lake water and rot and something sharp and chemical, like bleach.

I turn on my phone's flashlight. The boathouse is one long room built over the water. On either side, there's a narrow walkway of wooden planks, and in the middle, a rectangle of open water where a boat would sit. The slip. Dark water, lapping gently.

An old aluminum rowboat is pulled up onto the left-hand walkway, upside down. Beside it is the wheelbarrow. And beside the wheelbarrow, under the tarp, is the thing Celeste brought here last night.

I pull back the tarp.

Cinder blocks. Four of them. Brand new, still with orange price stickers from a hardware store. A coil of heavy chain. Zip ties, the thick industrial kind. A roll of duct tape. And a receipt from Hendrickson's Hardware in Virginia, Minnesota, dated four days ago.

I stand there, looking at it, and my mind does the math that my heart doesn't want to.

This isn't what happened to Maddie. This isn't old.

This is new. This is for someone who hasn't gone into the lake yet.

Grant. It has to be for Grant. She's going to lure him here, and then—

Or it's for me.

I back away from the tarp, and my heel catches on something, a gap between two planks near the edge of the slip, and I stumble and almost go into the water. I catch myself on the wall. And when I shine my light down at what tripped me, I see something glint in the crack between the boards.

Gold.

I crouch and pry it out with my fingernails. It's a bracelet. A delicate gold chain, the clasp broken, with a single tiny charm dangling from it.

A letter M.

Behind me, out on the dock, a board creaks.

Footsteps. Slow. Deliberate. Coming this way.

I switch off my light, and in the sudden total darkness, I hear the boathouse door swing open, and I smell something that doesn't belong in this place of rot and bleach and cold water.

Perfume. Something expensive. Something floral and cold.

Celeste's perfume.

sections.title: Chapter 20
sections.html:
Chapter 20

Rule #2: Never let anyone inside. No matter who they say they are.

I don't breathe.

I'm crouched on the far walkway, behind the overturned rowboat, the bracelet biting into my closed fist. The slip of black water lies between me and the door. A flashlight beam cuts through the dark, sweeping slowly over the walls. It touches the tarp, which I left thrown back. It pauses there.

It moves toward the rowboat.

I press myself flat against the planks. They're wet and freezing and smell like death. The beam passes over the hull a foot above my head.

Silence. Then a soft sound, almost a laugh.

"I know you're in here, Nora."

Her voice is so calm. So pleasant. Like we're meeting for lunch.

"I watched you walk down. You looked so brave." The beam swings back toward the door. "You're wondering who the blocks are for. Don't worry. I haven't decided yet."

The water laps at the pilings. My heart is so loud.

"Go back to bed," Celeste says. "Three more days. Follow the rules."

The door creaks shut. Footsteps on the dock, fading. Gone.

I stay there, flat on the wet boards, for a long time. Long after the footsteps are gone. Long enough that the sky through the cracks in the boathouse walls turns from black to charcoal.

Then I get up, and I walk back to the house, and I don't look behind me.

* * *

At six a.m., I walk Juniper down the gravel drive, like any other morning. At the end of it, Ortega's cruiser is parked in the trees with the engine running.

I get in the passenger seat. I put the freezer bag in his lap. And then I open my fist and show him the bracelet.

He goes very pale.

"Her mother gave us a list," he says quietly. "Of what Maddie was wearing. Gold bracelet, M charm. It was her grandmother's." He turns it over in his fingers like it might break. "Where?"

"The boathouse. Between the boards by the slip." I tell him about the cinder blocks. The chain. The receipt. Celeste's voice in the dark.

For a long moment, Ortega doesn't say anything. Then he pulls out his phone and starts dialing.

"This is enough," he says. "The phone, the bracelet, Dell's log. This is enough for a warrant. I'm calling the BCA in Duluth. They've got a dive team." He glances at me. "But I need to get this evidence to them myself. Chain of custody. That's three hours each way."

"Go."

"You're coming with me."

"If I leave now, she'll know." I look back up the drive toward the house. "She'll run. Or she'll clean everything. The blocks, the chain, the third floor. She's had a year of practice at making things disappear."

"Nora—"

"Grant can come get me tonight. Dell's watching the house. And I've got your code." I try to smile. "All quiet."

Ortega looks at me for a long time. Then he takes a second phone out of his glove box, a cheap black flip phone, and presses it into my hand.

"Prepaid. Only one number in it. Mine." His voice is rough. "She can't have hacked this one. You keep it on you. Every second."

I tuck it into my bra.

"There's a storm coming in tonight," he says. "A big one. Be careful."

sections.title: Chapter 21
sections.html:
Chapter 21

Rule #5: The lights facing the lake stay on from dusk to dawn.

The storm hits at six.

It comes across the lake like a wall, turning the water white and the sky the color of a bruise. Rain slams against all that glass. The pines along the shore bend and thrash. Somewhere, a tree cracks and falls with a sound like a gunshot.

At 6:40, Grant texts. A different number than before.

Phone died. Borrowed one. Roads bad but I'm coming. Be there by 8.

I stare at it. It sounds like him. It could be him.

I text his real number: Is this you?

No answer. Delivered, but no answer.

At 7:15, I text Ortega on the flip phone. Storm is bad. Grant says he's coming at 8. Something feels wrong.

His reply takes nine minutes. Highway 53 closed, trees down. I'm stuck outside Cotton. Dell there?

I look across the bay. Dell's house is just a smudge through the rain. His window is lit.

Yes, I type.

At 7:41, the power goes out.

It happens all at once. Every light in the house snaps off, the refrigerator stops humming, and the whole world goes dark and loud with rain. The lake-facing lights die with everything else. For the first time since I've been here, the house is not a lantern.

Rule five. Broken for me.

Juniper starts to growl. A low, deep rumble I've never heard from her before. She's standing at the top of the basement stairs, staring down into the dark.

"What is it?" I whisper. "What's down there?"

She doesn't stop growling.

I've never been in the basement. It wasn't in the rules, but it wasn't in the binder either. A mechanical room, I assumed. Furnace, water heater. There's a door at the bottom, I remember that from the house plans in the binder. A walkout door. Onto a path that leads down toward the water.

Toward the boathouse.

* * *

At 9:00 exactly, in the dark, the landline rings.

Old landlines don't need electricity. The phone company sends its own current down the wire. I learned that once, from a lawyer I worked for, during a case about a woman who called 911 during a blackout. I think about it now as I stand in the black kitchen listening to the phone ring, and ring, and ring.

I pick it up.

"Say it," Celeste says.

I take a deep breath. In my other hand, in the pocket of Grant's barn coat, my own phone is recording. I started the voice memo app at 8:58.

"No," I say.

Silence.

"I'm not saying it anymore. It's not all quiet. It hasn't been quiet since the day I got here." My voice doesn't shake. I don't know where the steadiness is coming from. Maybe from Maddie, laughing on the dock. "What happened to Maddie Kerr, Celeste?"

"You took something that belongs to me." Her voice is different now. Closer. Not the tinny sound of a cell phone far away. Clear. "From my chimney."

"It never belonged to you."

"Everything in that house belongs to me, Nora. Including you, for three more days." A pause. "Or less."

Headlights sweep across the front windows.

Someone is coming up the drive.

sections.title: Chapter 22
sections.html:
Chapter 22

Rule #2: Never let anyone inside.

The knocking is frantic. Fists on oak.

"Nora! Nora, it's Grant, open the door!"

I stand in the dark entryway with the bear spray in my hand. Through the frosted glass I can see his shape, backlit by his headlights, rain streaming off him.

"You texted me," I say through the door. "From a new number."

"What? No. You texted me. An hour ago. You said she was here and to come now."

Cold spreads through my chest.

C knows. She's here. Come now please.

It's the same message. The same trap. She's using it again.

"Grant," I say, "I didn't send you anything."

A long, awful silence on the other side of the door. And in that silence, behind me in the dark house, I hear the soft click of the basement door opening.

I unlock the front door and pull Grant inside. Rule two, gone. I slam it behind him and turn, and Juniper is barking now, wild, hoarse barks, and a flashlight beam blooms at the end of the hallway and blinds me.

"Rule two, Nora," says Celeste. "You really are hopeless."

* * *

She's wearing a long black raincoat, dripping on her own polished floor. Her pale hair is plastered to her head. In one hand she holds a flashlight. In the other, a gun.

Grant makes a sound in his throat. "That's mine. That's from my safe."

"Of course it is." Celeste smiles. "It's going to be very important that it's yours."

"Celeste." Grant steps in front of me. "Whatever you think is happening—"

"I know exactly what's happening." She tilts her head, considering us. "Here's the story, darling. You came up tonight in the storm, desperate. Your house sitter had found Maddie's phone in the chimney, where you hid it. You panicked. You came to take it back. There was a struggle." She shifts the gun toward me. "Poor Nora. And then I came home early, because I was worried, and I found you standing over her. And I had to defend myself."

"Nobody will believe that," I say.

"Everybody will believe that. They already believe half of it." She says it so simply. "That's why I chose you, Nora. A woman who lied her way into my house. Whose sister drowned while she watched. Nobody will look too hard at a girl like that. They'll just be sad, for a day, and then they'll move on."

"Like Maddie," I say.

Something flickers across her face. Irritation. "Maddie went upstairs too. Nineteen days. She found my little room and she saw what I'd been watching, all those nights with my husband, and she told me she'd go to the police. She was standing in my kitchen, in my house, drinking my water, and she said I'll tell him what you did." Celeste's voice doesn't rise. That's the most frightening part. "I only pushed her. She hit the corner of the island. It was very quick."

"You rowed her out to the point," I say. "You wrapped her in chain. And then you came back and bleached the boathouse."

"I'm very thorough."

"You weren't thorough enough," I say. "Her bracelet was stuck between the boards. And her phone isn't in the house anymore. Deputy Ortega has it. He's had it since six o'clock this morning. With your fingerprints on the bag."

For the first time since I met her, Celeste Aldridge looks uncertain.

It lasts less than a second. Then her face smooths back out, and her eyes go flat and empty, and I remember what Dell's wife said. There's nothing behind her eyes.

"Then it's a murder-suicide," she says. "Stories are flexible."

Grant lunges for her.

The gunshot in that glass hallway is the loudest sound I've ever heard.

sections.title: Chapter 23
sections.html:
Chapter 23

Rule #9: Never go to the boathouse.

Grant goes down.

I don't see where he's hit. I see him fall, and I see blood on the concrete, black in the flashlight beam, and I hear Celeste say damn it in the same tone you'd use for a spilled glass of wine. Then Juniper launches herself out of the dark and clamps her jaws around Celeste's wrist, and the flashlight goes spinning across the floor, and everything is shadows and screaming.

I run.

I don't decide to. My body just does it. I spray the bear spray in the direction of the screaming, and hear Celeste choke and curse, and then I'm through the kitchen and out the back door and into the storm.

The rain is like needles. The wind nearly takes me off my feet. I can't see anything. The house is dark, the lake is dark, the whole world is roaring. I stumble down the deck stairs and onto the slope and slip and fall and slide, and when I stop, I'm at the bottom, on my hands and knees on the frozen mud at the head of the dock.

Behind me, up the slope, a flashlight beam bursts out of the back door.

She's coming.

I fumble for the flip phone in my bra with numb fingers. Flip it open. Type two words. My fingers are shaking so badly it takes three tries.

All quiet.

Send.

The flashlight swings toward me. I scramble to my feet and run onto the dock, because it's the only direction left. The boards are slick. The lake is heaving on both sides, black water slopping over the edges. The boathouse is ahead of me, its door hanging open where I cut the lock last night.

A gunshot. Wood splinters beside my head.

I throw myself into the boathouse.

It's pitch black. I know the layout now. The narrow walkway. The open slip in the middle. The rowboat, the tarp, the cinder blocks meant for someone. I feel my way along the left wall, toward the back, where the dark is deepest.

The flashlight fills the doorway.

"Nora." Celeste is breathing hard. Her voice is ragged from the bear spray. Her eyes must be burning. Good. "This is where it's supposed to end anyway. I brought everything."

The beam finds me. She raises the gun.

And I do the only thing I can think of. I kick the stack of cinder blocks off the walkway and into the slip.

They hit the water with a huge, heavy splash. The chain is still looped through them. The coil whips across the boards, and snakes around Celeste's ankle where she stands on the edge, and the weight of four cinder blocks sinking into the lake yanks her off her feet.

She goes into the black water without a scream.

The flashlight goes with her. For a moment it glows under the surface, a sinking green star, and then it's gone.

I'm on my knees at the edge of the slip, staring down into nothing.

And my body does what it did fourteen years ago. It freezes.

I can't move. I can't breathe. I'm on the high rock at the quarry, and Ivy is under the water, and I am counting.

One.

Two.

Three.

No.

I go in.

sections.title: Chapter 24
sections.html:
Chapter 24

Rule #1: Never skip.

The cold is beyond cold. It's a wall that hits every nerve in my body at once. My chest locks. My vision goes white.

Then my body remembers how to be a body, and I kick.

It's black. Completely black. I can't see my own hands. But I can feel the chain. It's taut, running down into the depths, and I follow it hand over hand, down, down, my ears screaming with pressure, until my fingers close on fabric. The raincoat. A wrist. Celeste is thrashing, weakly, her ankle caught in the loop.

I claw at the chain around her leg. It's tight. My lungs are burning. I think: This is how I die. Saving her. The irony would kill me if the lake didn't.

Then the loop slips over the heel of her boot, and she comes free, and I kick upward with everything I have left, dragging her with me.

We break the surface in the slip. I'm gasping, choking. Celeste is limp and heavy. I get one arm over the edge of the walkway and hold her face above the water, and I hold on, and I hold on.

I don't know how long. Long enough that I stop feeling my hands.

Then there are lights. Real lights, red and blue, strobing across the rain through the cracks in the boathouse walls. And voices. And someone is on the walkway above me, a big man in a sheriff's department jacket, not Ortega, someone I've never seen before, and he grabs Celeste under the arms and hauls her out. And then another pair of hands grabs me.

Old hands. Strong ones.

"Got you," Dell Harker says. "I got you, girl."

* * *

It turns out Dell called 911 the moment the lake-facing lights went out. And when he saw the headlights, and then the flashlight bobbing down the slope, he called again. And then he got in his truck and drove around the bay in the storm on two bad knees, because, as he tells me later in the hospital in Virginia, "Waiting for help is how people end up in the lake."

A state trooper was only twelve miles away, stuck behind the same fallen trees as Ortega on Highway 53. My all quiet text went to Ortega, who called it in, and the trooper went around the closure on a logging road.
