Grant was shot through the shoulder. He lost a lot of blood on his own polished floor. But Juniper lay down beside him and wouldn't move, and the paramedics say the pressure of her body might be part of the reason he's still alive.

Celeste Aldridge was breathing when they pulled her out of the lake. She was charged two days later, in her hospital bed, with the murder of Madeline Kerr and the attempted murders of Grant Aldridge and Nora Vance.

The recording on my phone survived the lake. It was in the inside pocket of Grant's barn coat, in a sealed plastic sandwich bag I'd tucked it into before I walked down to the boathouse the night before, because I'm not stupid, and because I'd seen the water.

It's all there. I only pushed her. She hit the corner of the island. It was very quick.

* * *

The state dive team goes down at the deep hole by the point on a cold, clear morning four days later. I watch from Dell's dock, wrapped in a blanket, with Juniper at my feet.

They find her at eighty-seven feet.

Maddie's mother, Diane, comes up from Duluth the next day. She's small and gray-haired, with Maddie's wide smile, though it's hard to see it now. She hugs me for a long time in the parking lot of the sheriff's office and doesn't say anything, and I don't either. There isn't anything to say.

Before she goes, I give her the bracelet. The BCA has photographed it and logged it and doesn't need it anymore.

She holds it in her palm and looks at the little M for a long time.

"She always lost things," Diane says finally, and laughs, and cries. "Keys, sunglasses, phones. Every single thing. But she never lost this. Not once."

"She didn't lose it this time either," I say. "She left it for somebody to find."

sections.title: Epilogue
sections.html:
Epilogue

Rule #8: Burn nothing in the fireplace.

In December, it snows.

I have a small apartment in Duluth now, on the second floor of an old brick house with a view of Lake Superior if you lean far enough out the kitchen window. I have a job at a legal aid office downtown, helping people who can't afford lawyers fill out forms that decide the rest of their lives. The pay is bad. The work is good. When they called my old firm for a reference, somebody there must have read the news, because I got the job the next day.

I have a dog. Grant gave her to me when he got out of the hospital.

"She chose you," he said, standing awkwardly on my doorstep with his arm in a sling and Juniper's leash in his good hand. "Dogs know."

I don't know if that's true. But she sleeps at the foot of my bed every night, and some nights, when I dream about the water, I wake up with her head on my chest.

Deputy Ortega called once, in November, to tell me that the Hennepin County Attorney's office had decided not to pursue any charges related to a certain reference from a certain Mrs. Patterson of Edina.

"Didn't hear anything about it myself," he said. "Must have been a bad connection."

Tasha framed the newspaper article about the case and hung it in her bathroom. She says it's the only true crime story she knows where the house sitter wins.

* * *

The letter arrives on the first Saturday in December.

The envelope is plain white. The return address is the Saint Louis County Jail. My name and address are written in elegant, looping blue ink.

I stand in my tiny kitchen and hold it for a long time before I open it.

There's a single sheet of paper inside. Heavy, cream-colored stationery, the expensive kind. I don't know how she got it in jail. I suppose people like Celeste always find a way to get what they want.

It says:

Dear Nora,

I've had a great deal of time to think, and I wanted you to know that I don't hold it against you. You did what you had to. I would have done the same.

But I've been thinking about the quarry. About those thirty seconds.

The report says you counted. I found that detail so interesting. Most people who freeze don't count. Counting is a decision. It's a way of measuring something. Of waiting.

I read the rest of it too, you know. The part about the boy with the truck. The part where your mother told the deputy that you and Ivy hadn't spoken in a week.

I chose you for a reason, Nora. I always choose for a reason. I've spent my whole life looking at people through glass, and I know what I see.

We're not so different. You and I both know how long thirty seconds can be.

Warmly,

C.

* * *

My apartment doesn't have a fireplace.

But it has a gas stove, and a blue flame, and a small steel sink, and I hold the corner of the letter over the burner until it catches. I watch the cream paper curl and blacken. I watch her elegant blue ink turn to ash.

Rule number eight. Burn nothing.

I never was very good at following rules.

When it's gone, I run the water over the ashes and wash them down the drain. Then I stand at the kitchen window, looking out at the gray, frozen lake, with Juniper leaning warm against my legs.

Celeste is wrong. She has to be. I was seventeen, and I was scared, and I froze. That's all it was. That's all it's ever been.

Thirty seconds.

I've gone over them ten thousand times. One. Two. Three. The ripples closing like a mouth. My sister's hand breaking the surface once, reaching.

I've gone over them so many times I know every second by heart.

Which is why I know that Celeste is wrong.

Mostly.

About the Author

Sunday Pastores writes fast, twisty psychological thrillers about ordinary people who break the rules and find out why they existed. Rule Number Nine is Sunday’s debut novel.
